On the bright side, capital flowing from other sectors + semis to a successful $ANT IPO...

will eventually flow back into semi balance sheets over the long run. Circle of life. but for semis.

If we look at Anthropic's $900.9B of eventual purchase agreements:

- $AVGO + financing partners: $161.2B in Google TPU leases
- Google Cloud: at least $121.3B
- SpaceX: Up to $120.5B (ceiling, can be cut)
- Amazon: at least $110B
- Microsoft: $47.2B-$49.2B
- Nscale: up to $44.6B
- Lambda: ~$41.3BN ($34.9B can be cut)

With other identifiable counterparty deals such as:

- $MU (undisclosed), but supply agreement
- $RIOT: ~$28B+ $9.1B
- $WULF: ~$19B
- Akami: ~$11.6B (CPU cloud)
- Volta: ~$10B
- OnePWR: ~$3.4B
- $CRWV (undisclosed)
- Everwind (undisclosed)
- Likely $IREN (undisclosed)
- Zerra DC (undisclosed)

Outside the $900.9B, there's another:

- Additional Google TPU capacity: $125B-$150B estimated

- $AMD: over $20B if Anthropic takes the full initial tranche of Helios capacity

I'm actually personally longer term bearish on frontier lab valuations (I like OpenAI more if I had to pick one due to consumer stickiness). But raising a lot from IPO does help raise their counterparty status.

Regardless of how they utilize it, that's a lot of GPUs, TPUs, HBM, optical networking, and compute needed for the next 5+ years.

Serenity@aleabitoreddit
22:53 SGTInvesting
Now that we're close to 2027 it's a good idea to stress test downside scenarios where you have:

1. Capex cuts past 2028
2. Stranded Compute / DC Slowdowns
3. Finance deterioration (base case)
4. 2x+ rate hikes

Working in parallel and see what happens with valuations of AI longs.

If you see acceleration despite all 4, I'd argue that's an opportunity.

> Next-gen of photonics is one of the rare segments with an extreme rise in optical content and ASPs that can offset aggregate capex cuts.

Everyone’s moving into that space, including Elon Musk doing M&A, Marvell, Samsung and others with M&A… and we haven’t seen economic impact on emerging architectures even hit players from Celestial to Ayar + their suppliers yet.

If we look at a scenario where there's excess GPUs but power constraints:

We might see slowdown in aggregate accelerator/GPU/ASIC procurement, but your optical engines + light sources + switches players see acceleration.

Especially as incentive to replace power inefficient networking... since different (cheap BOM) optical architectures improves GPU utilization or even HBM requirements.

So value migrates to players more high-beta to architectural shifts.

If Celestial projections are $500m -> $1B, and we expect -30% aggregate capex cuts, I'd argue we'd still see upward revisions from Celestial over the next 2 years.

But financing with #3 matters a lot as seen with $AAOI dropping off of a $550M, vs. $COHR getting prepayments for capacity expansion from their customers.

Companies that rely on external foundries might be less sensitive to #3 since they're not as capex intensive.

On the other hand, companies in sectors have a lot of floating interest like certain Neoclouds, and require further financing might be the most impacted.

> Legacy and specialty memory is a different cycle that markets conflate with AI capex.

If consumer demand weakens but at the same time, players like Windbond exits DDR2, pricing durability is longer than markets expect.

> Wafer/substrate procurement such as ABF, SOI, InP are low cost but large downstream destruction if not secured, so we’ll likely see acceleration here as seen with $NVDA earnings call.

> qualification cycle players within bottlenecks remain very compelling, since first revenue in a large TAM, relative to MC is material to that company.

If a company is valued at $400m then they get a $200m of orders, it's more asymmetrical to a certain company than a rounding error to a $50B incumbent revenue.
_

There’s period of times where prices are dislocated from fundamentals from leveraged players getting wiped. I’d argue that time is now.

I disagree with a lot of the stupid "it's over takes" but I agree it's a good idea to haircut future capex expectations and forward valuations due to financing tightening + macro.

It's also good idea to see the nuances and stress test downside cases.

But TLDR: I'd argue next phase of AI infrastructure is going to be increasingly disconnected from aggregate AI capex growth.

I just personally wrote 4 things I'm using to stress test jointly some of the names I'm looking at, so I'm more comfortable waiting things out... despite seeing hedge funds getting liquidated left and right and overwhelming short positioning.

I personally see acceleration in more narrow parts of the supply chain, while markets treat the entire AI trade as one.

We'll see how things play out on longer horizons.

Venu@Venu_7_
14:56 SGTInvesting
TECH IS TRADING AT JUST 17X FORWARD EARNINGS. BUT IS IT REALLY CHEAP?

I’ve been seeing charts circulating lately showing that technology stocks are trading at some of their cheapest valuations in years.

Technology is up 13% this year, yet its forward P/E has fallen 32%.

Why? Earnings expectations have risen faster than stock prices.

But history tells us why investors should be careful:

- 2018: Micron traded at just 5.6x forward earnings near its peak before falling 56%.
- 2001: Low valuations didn’t prevent further declines as earnings estimates were revised lower.
- 2008: Tech’s forward P/E eventually fell to 9.9x.
- 2022: Valuations looked reasonable months before the market bottomed in October.

Remember, forward P/E is based on estimated future earnings, not guaranteed earnings.

And today, a significant portion of those expectations depends on continued AI spending.

A stock can look cheap fundamentally and continue getting cheaper technically.

I’m just playing devil’s advocate here since the majority have been focusing on the Price-to-Earnings argument. I just wanted to share a different perspective.

That being said, I don’t think 2026 is comparable to the dot-com bubble or the 2008 financial crisis. Companies like $GOOGL, $MSFT, and $NVDA are generating substantial profits.

Overall, I think this is more of a broader market correction playing out rather than a bubble or anything similar.

Valuation gives us context. Price action and earnings confirmation help us make better decisions.

“Neoclouds and frontier labs are seeing extraordinary demand for AI infrastructure, yet many are growing faster than their balance sheets and long-term credit profiles can support.”

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.

Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

Jensen

This is the kind of market environment where you don’t want to lean too bearish or too bullish.

Why not short?

- We’re already at oversold levels, and shorting into weakness offers limited reward with significant risk. Ideally, better shorting opportunities come when prices rally back toward declining moving averages and face resistance.

Why not go long?

- The Nasdaq and $SMH, the backbone of this bull market, are both trading below their 200-day SMAs, with signs of distribution and many market leaders also below their 200-day SMAs.

My approach? Stay neutral.

There’s no need to force positions in either direction. Let the market establish a clear trend before getting aggressive.

Sometimes, protecting capital and doing nothing is the best decision you can make.

David Ryan’s bear market rules are worth revisiting in the current market environment!

David Ryan, a three-time U.S. Investing Champion and student of William O’Neil, shares some valuable lessons:

- Get defensive when your portfolio falls 10-15% from its peak.
- Raise significant cash instead of fighting the downtrend.
- Focus on price action over fundamentals during market declines.
- Understand O’Neil’s three legs of a bear market.
- Don’t try to predict the bottom. Wait for the market to confirm a turn.

A valuable 3-minute lesson for every investor!

02:21 SGTInvesting
Technical analysis is supposed to remove emotions and bias from investing decisions, not justify them!

I'm increasingly noticing that quite a few people on X are using technical analysis incorrectly or allowing their personal biases to influence their conclusions. Not everyone, but definitely quite a few!

Let me make a few points:
- I define a stock's trend in two ways: short-term and long-term. When a stock trades above its 50-day SMA, I consider its short-term trend bullish. When it trades above its 200-day SMA, I consider its long-term trend bullish. The opposite applies when it trades below these moving averages.

- Once a stock loses its 200-day SMA, especially when that moving average starts declining, it's a warning sign of a potential Stage 4 downtrend. You never know where the bottom is, and that's why many successful investors & traders avoid buying stocks in established downtrends. One of the biggest lessons I learned from Stan Weinstein and William O'Neil!

- Do not use indicators like RSI to determine the trend. Oversold conditions can produce bounces, and overbought conditions can produce pullbacks, but RSI alone cannot define a trend. Look at $TTD, $NKE, and optical names like $AAOI. These stocks have experienced significant weakness despite oversold readings. Did being oversold automatically lead to a recovery? NO! So understand how to use RSI correctly.

- Anchored VWAP from earnings and major lows, such as the April 2025 tariff lows or 2022 market lows, can act as potential support. Anchored VWAP from major highs can act as potential resistance. These levels help us understand where buyers and sellers may react.

- All you really need is price action, volume, moving averages, and anchored VWAP. That's it! You don't need dozens of indicators to understand the trend.

And most importantly, please do not let your personal bias influence your technical analysis.

It won't just hurt you or your portfolio. It can also mislead newer investors and traders who are genuinely trying to learn!

The purpose of technical analysis is to understand what the market is telling you, not to make the market agree with your opinion!

$ABCL AbCellera CEO Carl Hansen shares some comments on the TAM of ABCL635:

“In the US alone, at any given time, we believe there is roughly 12 million women with moderate to severe VMS. Of that group, we expect there is about 20% that are either contraindicated or that cannot tolerate hormone therapy. All right, call that 2.2 million or so. That is already a market opportunity where you are not competing against the hormones.

The current list price, or the current net price of the small molecules, is about $5,000. That is about a $12 billion TAM. You might take a cut and say half people go get treatment, then it is $6.0 billion. That is already a very exciting market.

With the efficacy, we now think that we will have a bigger share of that market than we otherwise would have. We also think there is a compelling opportunity for the women that could use hormone therapy but either do not get sufficient relief or who decide that they do not want to take hormone therapy, either because of some adverse events they do not like or because they decide they do not want even the perception or the reality of a greater risk of oncology or of clotting.

There is not a small number of women that feel that way for good reason. There is an 80% of women there. If you captured even a quarter of that, that decided to take this option, you would basically double the market opportunity. If it was $12 billion, it would be $24 billion. That is all in the U.S.”

21:20 SGTInvesting
It's officially Nvidia's earnings day.

Today's earnings report and call will likely be the most watched earnings event in history.

We are watching two key things:

1. Do executives show any willingness to reinstate Jensen Huang

2. What has CHANGED from a business perspective

As of now, considering the information over the last 48 hours, we believe there is an <20% chance that Jensen returns.

Any indication that the probability is higher would be strongly bullish for the stock.

But, if not, then what has changed for Nvidia? With or without Jensen, this company remains one of the best businesses in the world.

We are looking to see if the company still expects revenue growth of 70%+ in FY2028, as management previously indicated.

We also look for any changes to AI infrastructure spending, demand for Blackwell and Vera Rubin chips, and the company's relationships with its largest customers.

If the fundamental outlook remains intact, then investors must ask: Does Jensen Huang's departure justify the -$750 billion in lost market cap?

We believe the market has already priced in a significant portion of the uncertainty surrounding Jensen's departure.

At the same time, the long-term AI infrastructure investment cycle remains intact, and Nvidia continues to sit at the center of it.

The burden is now on management to demonstrate that the business can continue executing at the same level without Jensen Huang.

More to come after earnings.

I want my stocks to go up.

Year-to-date hiring plans are up +34% YoY, to 655,304 workers.

Meanwhile, seasonal hiring announcements jumped +26% YoY, to 470,400, but remained 29% below the 660,150 recorded in 2024.

Seasonal positions now account for 72% of all hiring plans in 2026 and nearly 60% of the increase from last year.

Seasonal hiring is gaining momentum.

Serenity@aleabitoreddit
04:37 SGT quoteInvesting
Well, most of the time projections are noise and reactionary.

Like right now, sky-high projections for $ANT $700-$800B ARR over next few years is stirring up hype that I'd argue gets revised down later.

I do think it's important to model in capex forecasts dropping past 2028, due to the current reflexive nature of AI selloffs, rate hikes, etc.

The drawn out duration of Iran War doesn't help, Jensen leaving $NVDA certainty draws concerns over Nvidia's ecosystem.

But any catalyst, like if Iran War ends, can also change sentiment in a heartbeat (since bearish positioning is overwhelming).

- It's also clear financing has been tightening, since OpenAI only managed to raise $11B of their original $30B target so far.

- Markets are reacting enthusiastically to companies like $TE doing a $100M ATM today (nuking valuations)

- Although the "guppy" sector is probably the most sensitive to financing + rate changes.

On bright side... Neoclouds like $NBIS or $IREN seem to be adjusting by getting 100% capex prepayments or 90% GPU prepayments from their counterparties.

What I'd argue though is lower aggregate capex does not apply uniformly in supply chains.

- Mid-high range lasers for NPO/CPO are still sold out, as seen with $LITE now starting negotiations for 2030 capacity.
- MLCCs are seeing further tightening as content usage goes up for AI servers
- ABF substrates to InP substrates not really going anywhere.

If content per system goes up 10X-15X, capacity expands at 2-3X Y/Y, and capex drops 28%.

And content is so cheap that you can triple order and screw over competitors with wafer supply...

I'm pretty confident you'll see acceleration upstream in bottlenecks from optical components to substrates despite potential aggregate capex dropping.

Another rant is:

-I keep seeing this argument that "low P/E is a warning for cyclical that's going to crash" but these are just clown takes

Nobody seems to analyze duration scenarios like capacity expansion vs. content changes vs. demand. to actually see how long those earnings last.

If everyone seems to be exiting DDR2 lines, there's probably going be more tightness in 2027 despite consume demand weakening, even if it looks like it's low P/E.

- Also for concerns about CPO "delays", the same components like lasers are used for NPO. You'll still see 150-200mW NPO lasers or ELS NPO using the same 300–400+ mW lasers as CPO.

We'll just see acceleration with NPO as a bridge if CPO gets delayed and higher range lasers likely to remain in a severe shortage.

- Feels like markets have also completely discredited the merit of take/pay price floor LTAs as well that companies like SK Hynix to Samsung have.

If contractual agreements hold up, memory players look very undervalued.

TLDR:
- I think it's important to model in capex decreasing to numbers like -30% in hypothetical downside sceanrios.

Given AI profitability, it's clearly not sustainable for hyperscalers to aggregately increase capex $500B or $1T+ Y/Y, and that's never been a case I've argued.

- This is also not the same thing as demand destruction that markets are overreacting to now (which haven't happened yet).

- We can see demand revisions for GPUs, ASICs, and heavier cost parts of the supply chain, while acceleration increases elsewhere.

The nuances market miss by indiscriminately selling everything is going to present compelling opportunities when the dust settles. I think in the end institutions are probably going to end up owning more of the same names retail discovered early on.

Anyway, I think it's a good idea to try and survive until more earnings comes out.

Enterprise AI is entering a period of explosive growth.

The global enterprise AI market is now projected to grow from $31.5 billion in 2025 to a record $155.2 billion by 2030.

This represents a +393% increase in just 5 years, primarily driven by increased adoption of AI.

However, the next phase of this expansion will be more custom-tailored.

Companies are looking AI solutions tailored to their specific operations, with a growing emphasis on cost efficiency and control.

The AI Revolution is rapidly moving from experimentation to enterprise-wide implementation.
Yejin Choi @YejinChoinka · 17 Nov 2026, 01:01 SGT
Through my wonderful time at NVIDIA and Stanford, one question has kept me up at night:

Should the future of AI be monolithic or plural?

To answer this question, we’ve raised $110M to get started, backed by @MenloVentures, @MadronaVentures, @NVIDIA, @NEA, @KindredVentures,@Wing_VC, @aixventureshq, @Cisco, @Snowflake, among others.

Today, Carlos (@guestrin) and I are stoked to launch Noeri, a neolab to push the frontier of plural intelligence.

Noeri means “the plural of intelligence” or many intelligences.

The future of AI we root for is plural: a healthy ecosystem of many intelligences, in all sizes, strengths, and quirks.

Discovery, in particular, has always been plural: many curious minds, each devoted to their own question, often on roads less traveled.

Our path there is self-improving AI that:

-> learns continually on the job, closing the gap between what AI can do off the shelf and what the dynamic world demands

-> learns to use other AIs as tools and make new tools to overcome its own limitations

-> picks the right-sized model for your problem, at a fraction of the frontier cost

Then the power of intelligence, from the craftsmanship of making AI to ownership, can be in the hands of all.

@noeri_ai mission reflects who we are as the founding team. My career has been anything but linear, literally continual learning on the job. Carlos has devoted his career to building tools that empower people through AI.

We are all a bit contrarian, a bit adventurous, and above all, big believers in pluralism.

Join us to build this future together: noeri.ai
